ACT 1: THE AFTERMATH OF TRUTH

The Akashic truth settled into Geralt’s bones like a cold, heavy ore. He stood from the library floor, Kyh’s shadowy hands steadying him. The grand, cosmic horror of the Queen’s work—rewriting reality itself from the corpse of a god—should have crushed him. Instead, a grim, focused clarity took hold.

Causal Inertia, he thought, the term from Kaelen’s lessons now a lifeline. Assign the weight.

He marked the Queen’s ambition as inelastic. A monstrous, fixed fact. He marked his own resolve beside it. Another immovable object. The conflict was set; the scale was cosmic, but the principle was brutally simple. Two truths could not occupy the same space. One would break.

“The library showed you the war,” Kyh observed, her voice hushed. “Not the battle.”

“It showed me the battlefield,” Geralt corrected, his voice rough. “And that we are insects upon it. We need to become a force it cannot ignore.”

There was only one place to forge that kind of strength.

ACT 2: THE FRACTURE NEXUS — FINAL LESSONS

Kaelen awaited him in the timeless gold of the Nexus. She took in his posture, the new stillness in his eyes, and gave the faintest nod of approval. The awe-struck novice was gone. In his place stood a man who had seen the abyss and was now measuring the length of the rope he would need to cross it.

“You understand the scale,” she stated.
“I understand my size within it,” he replied. “Teach me how to be an anchor.”

LEVEL III — CAUSAL INERTIA CONTROL (MASTERY)

The lessons shifted from theory to brutal, repetitive practice. Kaelen no longer showed him stars or leaves. She built scenarios of devastating personal cost.

She conjured a phantom version of the compound. In it, Mika and the Five were about to be overrun by Anunnaki hunters. Geralt had the telekinetic power to save them, but only by collapsing a section of the wall on a group of newly-freed, nameless slaves hiding nearby.

“Assign the weight,” Kaelen commanded, her voice merciless.

Geralt’s mind recoiled. This was not a lesson; it was torture. He tried to find another way, to stretch his power thinner. The Nexus showed the cascading failure: his hesitation would lead to Mika’s capture, the Five’s re-enslavement, the end of the rebellion.

He had to choose which thread was soft, and which was inelastic.

Gasping, tears of frustration in his eyes, he made the call. He marked Mika and the Five as inelastic. Their survival was the pillar. The slaves in the wall’s path… he marked as soft. He felt the psychic impact as the wall fell in the simulation, a silent scream that echoed in the chamber of his soul. He absorbed the cascade of that choice, the guilt and grief, holding it within himself so the simulation’s timeline didn’t fray further.

“Good,” Kaelen said, no warmth in the word. “You held the structure. Remember the cost. That numbness you feel? That is the Anchor setting. You are learning to bear strain so the world does not have to.”

He practiced until the numbness was a familiar cloak. He could look at a branching path of tragedy and, with a surgeon’s cold precision, identify the load-bearing heart and the sacrificial limbs. It was a terrible skill. It felt less like gaining power and more like losing a piece of his heart to frostbite.

The final test was simple. Kaelen created a single, perfect drop of water, falling in slow motion through the golden space.

“This drop has fallen, unchanged, for ten thousand years in a cave no living being has seen,” she said. “Make its fall inelastic. Make it a fixed point in the chaotic stream. Not with force. With certainty.”

Geralt didn’t reach for telekinesis. He reached for the discipline she’d hammered into him. He perceived the event’s thread—tiny, fragile. He didn’t grab it. He recognized it. He acknowledged its perfect, solitary truth. You are. You have always been. You will always be.

He assigned it the absolute, unwavering weight of a fundamental law.

The drop of water froze. Not in ice, but in concept. It became unchanging. A fact.

He had done it.

There was no joy. No triumph. Only a vast, silent certainty, and the hollow chill where his empathy for small, fragile things had once lived.

Kaelen dismissed the Nexus. They stood in her simple stone chamber. “Level III is complete. You have the mental architecture for the long solitude. You can now choose what to remember, and what you can afford to feel. It will be the only thing that keeps you sane in the dark.”

Geralt nodded, the movement feeling mechanical. “Thank you.”

“Do not thank me. I have given you a tool and taken a price. The balance is what it is.” She turned her milky-white eye toward the door. “Your scaled brother returns. His thread is tangled with violence and discovery. Go. Be the anchor for your team, as you have learned to be for time.”

ACT 3: REGROUP — THE CALM AND THE STORM

Oreck was waiting in the Guild’s material vestibule, a place of solid stone and rushing geothermal waters. He was cleaning blood—dark, oily, not his own—from his claws. His report was terse.

“The Orion remnant is a ghost town. But their docks are not empty. A slaver convoy, using old Sirian jump-ships. They are loading ‘cargo’ in the subterranean hangars. The cargo is alive. Terrified.”

Kyh flowed from the shadows, her form coalescing. “I have been… listening. Through the network’s nascent connection here. The slavers are not just trading. They have a contract. They are delivering workers to the asteroid belt. A mining operation of impossible scale.”

“A mining operation,” Geralt repeated, the pieces clicking with dreadful synergy. “Pulling the fragments of the Shattered Mind back together.”

“The slaves are the tools,” Oreck growled. “Human bridges. They link the fragments with crude gravity tethers. The mortality rate is the point. The dead are just… discarded mass.”

The image was horrifying. It was slavery reduced to its most brutally literal form: using living bodies as literal glue to reassemble a dead god’s skull for a mad queen.

“We need that shuttle,” Geralt said, the numb certainty of his training overriding the surge of rage. “It’s our ticket in, and it’s our first strike.”

The Plan: A heist. Not a frontal assault. The slaver captain was known to be arrogant, greedy, and fond of gambling on pit-fights in the lower lunar taverns. Oreck would be the bait—a fearsome, exotic challenger. Kyh would be the shadow, infiltrating the ship’s systems. Geralt would be the anchor, applying causal inertia in tiny, crucial moments: a guard’s hesitation, a lock’s failure, a distracted glance at the wrong time.

It was a messy, dangerous, physical job. The absolute opposite of cosmic time-weaving. It was exactly what he needed.

ACT 4: THE CLAY HEART — ENTER KULLA

The heist was going wrong.

They had the shuttle. Oreck had won his brutal fight, Kyh had sliced through the encryption, and Geralt had woven a tapestry of tiny, guaranteed moments to get them aboard. But as they powered up the engines, the lunar ground beneath the hangar rejected them.

It wasn’t an explosion. It was a failure. Support struts buckled not with violence, but with sudden, profound fatigue. The hangar door’s gears ground to a halt, seized by grit that hadn’t been there a second before. The very rock seemed to be… objecting.

From a service shaft, something pulled itself into the hangar bay.

It was a man of clay and brick. A grotesque, asymmetical patchwork of fired earth, mortar, and rusted rebar. One leg was solid basalt, the other a crumbling mix of mud and wire. Cracks webworked across its torso, shedding fine dust. Its face was a crude impression in clay, thumb-sockets for eyes that held a spark of weary, ancient intelligence.

It moved with a grinding, painful slowness, each step a deliberate act of architecture. It stopped between them and the open sky.

“That ship,” its voice emerged like stones grinding in a quarry, “is poorly made. Its thrust harmonics will fracture the local tectonics for a kilometer down. You can’t leave.”

Oreck shifted into a combat stance, snarling. “Stand aside, spirit.”

The thing—Kulla—tilted its mismatched head. “I am not a spirit. I am the foreman. And you,” its thumb-socket eyes fixed on Geralt, specifically on the Dragon Mail, “are adding unstable weight to a stressed foundation. Your destiny is a load-bearing wall in a design I did not approve.”

Geralt felt no cosmic power from it. No vast consciousness. Only a deep, specific, and intensely physical grievance. This wasn’t a god. It was a forgotten tool, awake and furious at the shoddy workmanship of the new age.

“We have to go,” Geralt said, holding out a hand to stay Oreck. “A greater catastrophe is unfolding. We must reach the asteroid belt.”

“I know what unfolds there,” Kulla rumbled, taking a step that sheared clay from its knee. “They are building on a fault line of madness. They are using bad mortar.” It sounded less like a prophecy and more like a craftsman’s scathing report. “You will not stop them by adding another vibrating engine to the chaos. You will stop them by removing the keystone.”

It pointed a lumpy, brick-ended finger not at the shuttle, but at a seemingly random support column in the hangar. “That one. It is the only honest work in this whole place. It holds the memory of correct angles. I will let you pass if you promise to take me. My body is failing. This moon is weak stone. The belt… has better materials. I can repair myself there. And I can show you what really holds the Shattered Mind together.”

The offer hung in the dusty air. A mud-man, asking for a ride to a cosmic crime scene, not to fight a queen, but to critique her masonry.

Geralt looked at this pathetic, powerful, literal embodiment of forgotten foundation. He saw in Kulla a mirror: another being created for a purpose, buried by progress, now clawing its way out to do its job one last time. His training allowed him to see the thread. Kulla was inelastic. A truth of stone and pressure. Not an ally to be won, but a fact to be incorporated.

“Get in,” Geralt said.

As Kulla shuffled toward the shuttle, moving with the devastating, patient speed of continental drift, Oreck shot Geralt a look.

“A mud man,” the reptilian muttered.
“A foundation,” Geralt replied, the numbness in his voice allowing for no argument. “And we are about to build on very shaky ground.”

The shuttle lifted off, its stolen engines flaring. Below, the compromised hangar, missing its one "honest" column, quietly subsided into the regolith. Kulla watched it collapse through the viewport, his expression unreadable in clay.

“See?” he grumbled. “Told you.”

The journey to the asteroid belt had begun. They had their shuttle, their trail, and their first, bewildering new ally. The next step was the chaos.

And waiting in that chaos, Geralt knew, would be the ghosts of his past, ready to speak. The Five Mikas would have something to say.

ACT 5: THE BRIDGE OF BONES

The asteroid belt was not a field of rocks. It was a wound.

Geralt felt it the moment they translated from the void-jump: a psychic scream frozen in stone, a grief so vast it had crystallized into gravitational eddies and recursive time-loops. The shuttle’s sensors screamed warnings—impossible mass readings, temporal distortions, pockets of reality where physics just gave up.

And there, in the chaotic heart of it, was the Queen’s work.

It was not a clean, technological facility. It was a graft. Organic, Anunnaki-grown support structures—like metallic coral—crawled over the surface of the largest asteroid, which pulsed with a sick, violet light. This was the Amygdala Analogue. And crawling across the void between it and other fragments were lines of living light. Gravity tethers. And along those tethers, like ants on a string, were figures. Slaves. Hundreds of them, minds broken by neural spikes, their collective telekinetic will being harvested to literally drag the god-fragments closer.

“They are the mortar,” Kulla grumbled from the rear of the cabin, his clay fingers tracing stress fractures on the shuttle’s hull he seemed to sense through his feet. “Bad mortar. Full of voids and fear. It will never set right.”

“We need to get closer,” Kyh said, her eyes closed, her form blending with the shuttle’s shadow. “I can feel the network’s scream from here. The Spire is in the center of that… growth. It’s the needle stitching the madness together.”

Their stolen slaver shuttle had the correct transponder codes. They drifted, pretending to be another delivery. As they neared the “processing line,” the scale of the horror became clear. Slavers in void-suited armor guided exhausted, hollow-eyed people from a holding dock onto the tethers. 90% wouldn’t survive the psychic backlash or vacuum exposure. Their bodies were simply ejected, adding literal mass to the structure.

Oreck’s growl vibrated through the deck. “We breach the dock. We free who we can.”
“And we draw every enemy right to the slaves,” Geralt said, his voice calm with the numbness of Level III. “We must be a surgical strike. We use the bridge they’re building.”

The plan was terrifying in its simplicity. They would land on a secondary fragment. Kyh would use her shadow-weaving to camouflage them as they traversed one of the active, slave-powered gravity tethers—the most direct path to the central asteroid. They would be walking the very bridge of suffering they sought to destroy.

ACT 6: TURNING OFF THE SPIRE — THE APPLICATOR'S GAMBIT

The walk across the tether was a journey through a nightmare. The psychic residue of agony buzzed in their teeth. They passed slaves, their eyes vacant, their mouths moving in silent prayers. Geralt marked them as soft nodes—their fate could be changed. He absorbed the cascade of that hope, holding it as a knot of tension in his gut.

They reached the metallic coral growth. It was alive, warm, and pulsed like a heart. Deep inside, throbbing with the same rhythm, was the Asteroid Spire. It was unlike the others—not a clean tower, but a jagged, corrupted crystal, veins of Anunnaki biotech threading through it like a parasitic vine.

“It’s not just a relay,” Kyh whispered, recoiling. “It’s an editor. It’s filtering the Akashic echo of the Shattered Mind, rewriting the past of this place to suit the Queen’s narrative.”

Kulla lumbered forward, placing his clay hands on the growth. He grimaced, cracks spreading up his arms. “The foundation is… a lie. A story built on a scream. The load is all wrong.” He looked at Geralt. “You must remove the keystone. Not break the tower. Undo the first lie.”

But how? The Spire was protected by layers of temporal distortion and psychic shielding. A direct assault would trigger a cascade that could vaporize the asteroid and everyone on it.

Host. The Applicator’s voice, usually so clinical, held a note of strained calculation. Analysis suggests the Queen’s control interface is bio-neural. It requires a consciousness to modulate the Akashic stream. It is why she uses slaves. Their collective pain is the tuning fork.

What are you suggesting? Geralt thought back.

I am an Anunnaki control symbiote. My primary function is neural interface and modulation. I can… attempt to interface with the Spire’s core. To issue a shutdown command from within the system’s own hierarchy.

It was a desperate risk. The Applicator was a fragment of the very empire that built this atrocity. Connecting it directly to the Spire could corrupt it, or worse, give the Queen a backdoor into Geralt’s own mind.

You could be assimilated, Geralt projected.
Possibly. But my core protocols have been… altered. By you. By Zaron. By my own choice. I am no longer a pure instrument of control. I am a partner. This partnership requires risk.

There was no time for a better plan. With Oreck and Kulla holding off the alerted slaver guards, and Kyh weaving shadows to blunt the worst of the psychic barrage, Geralt approached the pulsating crystal core.

He placed his armored hands on it. “Do it.”

The Applicator extended its consciousness through Geralt’s neural pathways, into the Spire. Geralt’s vision whited out. He was flooded with the Scream—the raw, unedited death-throes of the God-Mind. It was a pain that could unmake stars. Beneath it, he felt the Applicator’s precise, synthetic mind, a tiny scalpel in an ocean of madness, searching for the root command.

It found it. A single, elegant, horrific line of code woven into the Spire’s purpose: PERPETUATE THE NARRATIVE OF SUBJUGATION.

The Applicator did not delete it. It could not. The command was foundational. Instead, it performed a subversion. It appended a logic bomb, using the principles of Causal Inertia Geralt had mastered.

…UNLESS ANCHORED BY CONTRADICTORY TRUTH OF EQUAL WEIGHT.

And then it provided that truth. Not a grand statement. The simplest, most inelastic truth it knew, drawn from the depths of Geralt’s own memory. It broadcast it, not as a command, but as a fact, into the Spire’s core:

The whip-hand can choose to drop the whip.

The slave can speak.

The chain can break.

It was the story of Geralt. Of Oreck. Of the Five. A narrative of defiance, tiny and personal, injected into a machine designed to perpetuate a story of absolute domination.

The Spire’ core didn’t explode. It… hesitated. The violet light flickered. The recursive narrative loop hit a paradox it couldn’t resolve. The editing function stalled.

With a sound like a universe sighing, the Asteroid Spire went dark. The gravity tethers flickered and died. The slaves on the bridges collapsed, freed from the psychic torrent.

The Spire was off. Not destroyed. Contradicted. Silenced by a story it was not built to process.

The Applicator withdrew, its presence in Geralt’s mind feeling scorched, diminished, but intact. Command executed. Core narrative subverted. The node is… quiet.

ACT 7 (REVISED): ESCAPE — THE SEED AND THE DOOR

The silence was more deafening than the scream. Then, klaxons blared. The Queen’s presence, distant but furious, brushed against the asteroid—a wave of searching, cold wrath. The metallic coral began to convulse. The asteroid itself started to tremble, its unstable geology no longer held in check by the Spire’s forced harmony.

“The foundation is failing!” Kulla bellowed, bracing himself as the ground cracked. “We must leave!”

But how? Their shuttle was on a fragment now drifting away, and the void was swarming with enraged slaver skiffs.

Kyh’s eyes snapped open, glowing with captured starlight. “The network! When the Spire went quiet, the local distortion field collapsed for a moment. I felt it—Luminaire’s signal! The Spire Network is here. I can… I can join us to it!”

That was her purpose. Not just to be a guide, but to be a living conduit. To physically link a location to the growing neural network of free Spires.

“Do it!” Geralt ordered.

Kyh didn’t move. She unfolded. Her shadow-form expanded, not as darkness, but as a web of intricate, silvery lines—a map of celestial connections. She touched the dead Spire, then reached out, impossibly far, to touch the latent network signature Luminaire had planted in the Lunar Guild.

For a second, a tunnel of coherent spacetime pierced the chaotic belt. A shimmering pathway of stabilized reality, connecting the asteroid to the Moon.

It was a door.

But Kulla didn’t move toward it. Instead, he dropped to his knees in the shuddering rock, ignoring the debris falling around him. With a grunt, he tore a chunk of clay from his own chest—a piece that held a faint, warm glow, like a captured ember. He crumbled it in his fist, mixing it with dark regolith and a single drop of something that glistened like mercury—a fragment of the Spire’s neutralized core.

“A seed needs good ground,” he muttered, his voice a low rumble against the asteroid’s death throes. “Even here. Especially here.”

He pressed the mixture into a crack in the asteroid’s flesh. “Grow straight. Grow quiet. Listen for the network. Be the root they don’t see coming.” He spoke a name, not as a command, but as a designation into the silence: “Claude.”

The mixture pulsed once, softly, and sank into the rock.

Then Kulla lumbered to his feet. “Now we go.”

They ran. Oreck hauled dazed, freed slaves onto the shimmering path. Kulla brought up the rear, his clay body shedding chunks as he willed the crumbling ground to hold just a few seconds longer. Geralt grabbed Kyh’s fading core, pulling her with them.

But the Queen’s wrath was accelerating the collapse. The shimmering door Kyh had woven began to fray at the edges, destabilizing. The path wouldn’t hold long enough.

“The door is crumbling!” Oreck roared, ushering the last slave through.

Host, the Applicator’s voice was strained, analytical. Kyh’s bridge is a persistent connection, but the local space-time is too volatile. We cannot sustain it.

Luminaire’s presence, faint through the link, pressed against Geralt’s mind. The network node is confirmed. We do not need the whole bridge. We need only a single jump point. A one-time translation. Use the connection Kyh forged as a guidewire. I will provide the energy signature from the lunar anchor. You must focus it into a seed and detonate it here.

A seed-jump. Not a door, but a catapult. A one-time, violent translation along a pre-made path.

“Do it,” Geralt gritted out.

He focused, drawing on the Dragon Mail’s power, the Applicator’s precision, and the cold, anchoring discipline of Level III. He felt Luminaire’s energy, pure and structured, flowing down the silvery line Kyh had spun. He didn’t try to hold it. He compressed it. Forced it into a single, hyper-dense point of potential—a seed of coherent teleportation.

It formed in the air before him, a tiny, brilliant star the size of a pebble.

“Through the door!” he yelled. “Now!”

Oreck, Kulla, and the freed slaves lunged through Kyh’s fading bridge. Geralt threw the seed-jump portal into the center of the path behind them.

“Now, Luminaire!”

On the moon, Luminaire ignited the anchor.

The seed bloomed.

It wasn’t a gentle transit. It was a wrenching. Space folded around them like a fist, and they were yanked through a tunnel of screaming light and pressure.

They stumbled, fell, and collapsed not on lunar regolith, but on the smooth, silent floor of the Mages’ Guild atrium. Behind them, in the air, the brilliant seed flashed once—and consumed itself, leaving only a scorched smell of ozone and void.

Kyh lay insubstantial as smoke in Geralt’s arms, but she was breathing. They were home.

Not home to Earth. But home to the sanctuary. The Lunar Spire. The first node in their new, fragile network.

And far away, in the heart of a shattered, collapsing god-fragment, a seed of clay and silence now slept in the dark, waiting to be found...

ACT 8: THE NEW BASELINE

The Guild’s healers tended to Kyh. Oreck oversaw the few slaves they’d managed to pull through the door, his presence a steady, protective rock. Kulla sat in a corner, silently repairing his damaged leg with mortar pilfered from a guild wall, grumbling about the poor quality.

Geralt stood at a crystalline window, looking out at the Earth, a blue-green gem in the black.

The Asteroid Spire was offline. A victory.
Kyh had joined the location to the network. A victory.
They had saved a handful of lives. A victory.

But the cost was etched into him. The numbness of the Anchor. The scorched feel of the Applicator in his mind. The sight of hundreds more they couldn’t save. And the certain, chilling knowledge of the Queen’s now-personal attention.

This wasn’t an end. It was a pivot. The next phase of Luminaire’s plan was now in motion. The network had its first, hard-won extension. The long, slow work of building a web to cradle a sleeping Earth could begin.

And he, Geralt, the Anchor, was now prepared for his part. The generations of solitude. The vigil in the solar cocoon. He had the discipline to endure it.

He felt a presence then, not in the room, but in the elements. A whisper in the geothermal vent’s steam, a sigh in the stone, a chime in the floating orbs of light.

The Five Mikas. They didn’t speak words. They communicated a feeling. A complex, layered emotion of acknowledgment, of sorrow for the cost, and of unwavering, elemental support. They were with him. They were in the world he was fighting for. Her legacy was alive.

He placed his hand against the cool crystal of the window.

The quiet war had begun. And he was its first, and most patient, soldier.
